Big Buddha (Wat Phra Yai) is the golden seated Buddha on Koh Fan, a small islet joined by a causeway to Koh Samui's north-east coast, about 3 km north of the airport. Entry is free and the temple is open every day from 07:00 to 18:30. Cover your shoulders and knees, take your shoes off on the upper platform, and plan on 45–60 minutes, or longer if you add Wat Plai Laem, about 1 km to the east.

Map and directions

Big Buddha sits on the north-east tip of the island, where Route 4171 loops between Bang Rak, Plai Laem and Choeng Mon. From the ring road (Route 4169) near the airport, follow the signs for "Big Buddha" north for about 3 km; the golden statue is visible from the road long before you reach it. The causeway starts by the stalls and the car park.

Get directions: open Big Buddha in Google Maps. Other points on the same map: Wat Plai Laem (about 1 km east), the Big Buddha pier for Haad Rin boats (a short walk west along the shore) and Bang Rak, also called Big Buddha Beach.

What Big Buddha is, and why it matters

Wat Phra Yai means "Temple of the Big Buddha". It is an active Buddhist temple, not a monument park, and the statue is Samui's best-known landmark. The image shows the Buddha seated in the "calling the earth to witness" posture (Maravijaya): the right hand rests on the knee and reaches towards the ground. In the story behind the pose, the Buddha touches the earth to call it as witness to his merit when the demon Mara challenges his right to enlightenment. It is the most common seated posture in Thai temples.

For islanders the temple is a place to make merit, not only a photo stop. You will see local families bringing flowers, candles and incense, monks giving blessings, and Thai visitors kneeling to pray before they take any photos. Loy Krathong is one of the busiest nights of the year here.

How tall is it? Figures of 12 m and 15 m both appear in guidebooks and signs, and we have not found an official measurement we trust, so we don't quote one. Either way, it dominates the headland and is easy to pick out from boats crossing to Koh Phangan. The construction date is quoted inconsistently as well, so we leave it out until we can confirm it with the temple.

What you'll see, step by step

  1. 1. The approach and stalls. The road ends at a small square of souvenir shops, snack stands and drinks stalls at the foot of the causeway. Prices are set for visitors; a bottle of water costs more here than at a 7-Eleven. This is also where you can rent or buy a sarong if you forgot to cover up.
  2. 2. The causeway. A short, flat walk across the water to Koh Fan. On calm days you can see fish in the shallows and boats moored off Bang Rak.
  3. 3. The naga staircase. Two serpent (naga) balustrades run up either side of the main staircase to the platform. It is a steady climb rather than a hard one, but there is little shade by midday. Shoes come off at the top of the steps; there are racks.
  4. 4. The platform and the statue. The terrace runs around the base of the Buddha, with views over Bang Rak bay to Koh Phangan on clear days. Walk around clockwise, the respectful direction in Thai temples.
  5. 5. Bells and merit-making. Rows of bells hang along the terrace for visitors to strike for good luck. [check] You can buy flowers, candles and incense as offerings, and put money in the donation boxes that fund the temple.
  6. 6. Back at the base. Smaller shrines and images sit around the foot of the islet. Monks often give blessings during the day; a small donation is customary but not required.

Good to know: toilets at the base are few and basic. Use the ones in Bang Rak or at a café if you can.

Big Buddha dress code and etiquette

Staff turn away visitors in beachwear, so dress before you arrive. The rules are the same as at every temple on Koh Samui:

  • Cover shoulders and knees. T-shirts, light trousers, long shorts below the knee or a long skirt are fine. No bikinis, vests, crop tops or swim shorts.
  • Bring a sarong. It is the easiest fix for everyone. Sarongs are sold at the stalls at the base for a few hundred baht. Whether the temple still lends wraps free of charge varies, so don't count on it. [check]
  • Shoes off on the upper platform and before entering any room with a Buddha image.
  • Never point your feet at the Buddha or at monks. When you sit, tuck your feet behind you or to the side.
  • No climbing or posing on or against Buddha images, and no photos with your back turned and arms raised in front of the statue. Thai law treats disrespect to Buddha images seriously.
  • Women should not touch monks or hand them anything directly; place the item on a cloth or table, or pass it via a man.
  • Keep your voice down and don't fly drones over the temple.

More on temple manners across the island: Koh Samui temples and etiquette and Thai culture and traditions.

Best time to visit and photo tips

Early morning (07:00–09:00) is quietest and coolest. Tour vans start arriving around 09:30 and the platform is busiest until early afternoon. Late afternoon (16:00–18:30) brings softer light and cooler stone underfoot; the temple closes at 18:30, so arrive by 17:30 if you want time on the platform.

  • The classic shot: from the start of the causeway, with the staircase leading the eye to the statue.
  • Silhouette: from the Bang Rak shore west of the islet in the last hour before closing.
  • Midday: the gold glare is harsh and the stone gets hot on bare feet. Bring sunglasses and water.

By season: the dry, calm months are February to April. October to December is the north-east monsoon, and November is the wettest month (about 445 mm of rain), with sudden heavy showers; the platform has no cover, so time your visit between showers. Peak crowds come in July–August and from mid-December to February.

Loy Krathong at Big Buddha (Tuesday 24 November 2026)

Loy Krathong falls on Tuesday 24 November 2026, the full moon of the twelfth lunar month. Big Buddha and Chaweng Lake are the two classic spots on Samui to float a krathong, a small raft of banana trunk and leaves with a candle, incense and flowers. Families gather at the causeway and along Bang Rak beach from early evening; expect traffic and full parking from about 18:00.

  • Choose an eco krathong made of bread or banana leaf, not foam. Vendors near the causeway sell them on the day.
  • Sky lanterns are banned on Koh Samui because of the fire risk. Don't release one.
  • Loy Krathong is not an alcohol-ban day, and it is not a public holiday.
  • The same night is a Full Moon Party on Koh Phangan. If you want both, float your krathong early and join our Full Moon Party speedboat (1,400 THB return). See Loy Krathong on Koh Samui for the full programme.

The Big Buddha pier and boats to Koh Phangan

The small pier just west of the causeway is where the Haad Rin Queen ferries and speedboats leave for Haad Rin on Koh Phangan, the Full Moon Party beach. Crossings take about 30–50 minutes depending on the boat, with fares of roughly 200–500 THB one way. Timetables change by season and around party nights, so check departures the day before. Several different piers in this area are all called "Bangrak pier", so always check the exact pier name on your ticket.

For party nights, our door-to-door Full Moon Party speedboat includes the return boat and hotel pickup from most areas of Koh Samui; Nathon, Lipa Noi, Taling Ngam, Bang Kao and Thong Krut add 400 THB per person return. Party entry (about 200 THB) is paid at the gate; we don't sell entry tickets. Groups can book a private Full Moon speedboat. More options: Koh Samui to Koh Phangan.

Parking, facilities and accessibility

  • Parking: the car park at the foot of the causeway is the only sizeable one. Any parking fee is small and paid in cash on the spot. [check] On weekend evenings the approach road becomes a small market and parking runs out; come by scooter or Grab.
  • Scooters: park in the marked rows, lock the steering and take your helmet with you or lock it under the seat.
  • Food and drink: snack stalls at the base; seafood restaurants along Bang Rak beach a few minutes away.
  • Accessibility: the stalls, causeway and lower terrace are flat and manageable with a wheelchair or pushchair. The statue platform is reached only by the staircase; there is no ramp or lift. Visitors who can't manage stairs still get a good view of the statue from the causeway.
  • With children: the causeway is open to the water on both sides; keep small children by the hand.

A good half day: Big Buddha at 07:30, Wat Plai Laem at 08:30, a swim at Choeng Mon, lunch, then rest. In the evening, Fisherman's Village is a 15-minute ride. Our temple guide has a full north-east route that adds the hilltop chedi at Khao Hua Jook above Chaweng.

Times are without traffic; allow more in Chaweng in the evening and on Fridays near Bophut. Samui taxis don't use meters, so agree the fare before you get in. Grab works well in this part of the island. Songthaews (shared pickup trucks) run along the ring road for about 30–80 THB for locals (visitors are often asked 50–120 THB), are cash only and mostly stop by 20:00–22:00. If you rent a scooter, you need an International Driving Permit with the motorcycle category and a helmet; the helmet fine is up to 2,000 THB. See getting around Koh Samui and motorbike rental.

On a tour: most shared 4x4 jungle safaris stop at Big Buddha along with Na Muang waterfall, Wat Khunaram and Hin Ta and Hin Yai (market price about 1,700 THB). See our Koh Samui jungle safari page and enquire on WhatsApp.
